title: Retrieve the control first; restore only after you name what failed
goal: Retrieve the Days45–50 control chain, then fill the table-recovery gap with product-specific history and retention limits.
tag: Certification cycle 7 · retrieval and gap session · table recovery
concept:
A guardrail prevents a car from leaving the road. A tow truck recovers it afterward. They solve different problems.

Days45–50 built preventive and detective controls: preserve bad rows, keep array position, inspect join plans, mask values, bind workload identity, and test the whole chain. Today adds a missing recovery control. After an accidental delete, first identify the last known-good table state. Restore or clone only after proving the target point and retention boundary.
example: orders_silver had 1,000 rows. Statement delete-51 removed 880, leaving 120. The safe response is not “rerun everything.” Inspect history, verify the earlier state, create a recoverable copy where possible, reconcile counts, then choose the production cutover.

use_case.when: Use history-based recovery when a governed Delta or Snowflake table was changed or dropped and the required historical files are still retained.
use_case.example: A production cleanup job deletes 880 of 1,000 order rows; the incident team needs a verified pre-delete table state without replaying every upstream source.
use_case.decision: Prefer a historical clone for investigation when the product supports it. Restore in place only after impact, downstream readers, retention, permissions, and reconciliation are understood. Replay source data when history is unavailable or external effects also need repair.

practice: Choose the failure and retained-history state. Predict whether the control prevents, detects, recovers, or cannot repair the loss.
boundary: The local Python and JavaScript models use row counts and named versions. They do not execute Delta RESTORE, Snowflake Time Travel, VACUUM, Fail-safe, permissions, concurrent writes, streaming checkpoints, clones, costs, lineage, downstream side effects, or disaster recovery.

A retained historical state plus a verified recovery procedure
A larger broadcast threshold
Another masking policy
Masking governs reads; it does not restore deleted rows.
Why verify a clone or historical query before an in-place restore?
To prove the target state and reconciliation before changing production again
To make both products use identical syntax
To bypass retention
Recovery should reduce uncertainty before the next destructive change.
When must the team replay source data instead?
When required history or files have expired or external effects also need reconstruction
Whenever a query is slow
Whenever the analyst role is masked
History-based recovery is bounded by retained state and protected effects.

product_sections.title: Snowflake: query before the statement, clone the historical table, then reconcile
product_sections.html:
First-minute product recall: Day28 separated authentication from authorization; Day45 separated validation from loading; Day48 applied query-time masking. Recovery is a separate retained-history decision.

-- Snowflake SQL; not executed in productSELECT count(*) FROM orders_silver BEFORE(STATEMENT => 'delete-51');CREATE TABLE orders_silver_recovered CLONE orders_silver  BEFORE(STATEMENT => 'delete-51');

Time Travel can query or clone a historical state within retention. Standard Edition defaults to one day; permanent objects on Enterprise Edition and above can be configured up to 90 days. UNDROP is for a dropped object, not an ordinary DELETE.

title: ScopedValue ends with the call; ThreadLocal can outlive it
goal: Use Java 25 ScopedValue for bounded, one-way request context without leaking mutable thread state.
concept:
A visitor badge works only while you are inside the building. A sticky note left on a shared desk can be read by the next visitor.

Java 25 ScopedValue binds an immutable context for one dynamic call scope. Far-away callees can read it, but they cannot overwrite that binding. When the call ends—normally or exceptionally—the binding disappears. This is narrower than a mutable ThreadLocal whose value lives until code removes it.

// Java 25 API; not executed in this runtime
static final ScopedValue<RequestContext> CTX = ScopedValue.newInstance();
ScopedValue.where(CTX, ctx).run(() -> handleOrder());
example: Request req-51 binds tenant bank-a. A repository method reads that value without every intermediate method accepting a context parameter. After handleOrder returns, reading CTX outside the scope is invalid; the next request cannot inherit bank-a accidentally.

use_case.when: Use ScopedValue for immutable request context that must flow down a bounded Java call tree, especially with virtual threads or structured concurrency.
use_case.example: Pass tenant, trace, and policy context through a Java API handler into repository and audit code without mutable thread-local cleanup.
use_case.decision: Prefer ordinary method parameters when only a few layers need the value. Use a small immutable record when several context fields travel together. Do not use ScopedValue as a global cache or mutable session store.

practice: Step into, rebind, and leave nested request scopes. Predict the value visible at each call depth.
boundary: The recorded Python stack and browser model illustrate dynamic scoping only. They do not execute Java 25 ScopedValue, virtual threads, StructuredTaskScope inheritance, JVM access control, exceptions, performance caches, or thread handoff.

title: Start another initiative only when one leaves the system
goal: Use a portfolio WIP control to expose priority conflicts and finish cross-team platform work.
concept:
Opening ten restaurant orders at once does not make ten meals arrive sooner. It fills every counter with half-finished plates.

Work in progress (WIP) is work that has started but is not finished. An explicit WIP control creates a pull rule: start another initiative only when capacity becomes visible. At Distinguished Engineer scope, this makes executive priority trade-offs concrete across teams instead of hiding them inside multitasking.
example: Your platform portfolio has four active slots: lineage, schema contracts, Airflow migration, and cost controls. A fifth request—real-time quality—arrives. Starting it immediately would split specialists across five partially delivered outcomes. The pull rule asks leaders to finish, stop, or explicitly expedite one item first.

use_case.when: Use a portfolio WIP control when critical engineers are spread across many initiatives and cycle time grows while everything remains 'in progress.'
use_case.example: Limit cross-team data-platform initiatives to four active outcomes, with one explicit expedite policy for regulatory work.
use_case.decision: Choose a control that reflects the actual shared bottleneck, not an arbitrary team count. Make exceptions visible and review item age; a WIP number without finish policies or leadership trade-offs becomes theater.

practice: Change active work, the WIP control, and completions. Predict whether a new initiative can be pulled.
boundary: The arithmetic model treats initiatives as equal slots. It omits skill mix, dependencies, uncertainty, urgency, item size, service-level expectations, funding, morale, and probabilistic throughput. WIP control informs a decision; it does not choose strategy.

title: Stateless MCP needs explicit application handles—not hidden sessions
goal: Scale MCP 2026-07-28 across instances while keeping state visible in tool arguments.
tag: GenAI harness engineering · MCP 2026-07-28 stateless core
concept:
A coat-check ticket lets any attendant retrieve your coat. You do not need the same attendant to remember your face.

MCP 2026-07-28 removes the protocol session and Mcp-Session-Id. Each request is self-describing and may reach any server instance. If a tool needs application state across calls, return an explicit handle such as basket_id and require the model to pass it next time. The handle makes state part of the tool contract rather than invisible transport memory.
example: basket/create lands on instance A and returns b-51. basket/add lands on B with basket_id=b-51. B resolves the application record from the shared business store. Without the handle, B must reject the call; sticky routing is not the contract.

use_case.when: Use explicit handles when a modern stateless MCP tool workflow spans calls but the business operation still needs durable application state.
use_case.example: A data-quality agent creates a draft rule set, receives rule_set_id rs-51, then validates and publishes that exact draft through later tools on any server instance.
use_case.decision: Keep one-shot tools fully stateless. Mint opaque, authorized, expiring handles for multi-step workflows. Use the Tasks extension for durable asynchronous work rather than inventing a transport session.

practice: Route create and add calls to different instances. Remove or alter the handle and predict the result.
boundary: The Python and browser models use one in-memory dictionary. They do not implement MCP transport, server/discover, _meta, authorization, tenant binding, opaque IDs, expiry, persistence, encryption, retries, concurrency, or the Tasks extension.

title: A cleaner dielectric lets a 2D transistor switch with less uncertainty
goal: Understand a newly published 2D CFET result while separating measured devices from manufacturing readiness.
tag: Technology breakthroughs · new peer-reviewed research · November 11, 2026
concept:
A light switch should change state at the same point every time. If dust inside the switch traps charge, the trip point wanders depending on which direction you moved it.

A Nature paper integrates transferable single-crystal anatase TiO₂ with atomically thin MoS₂ and WSe₂ channels. The cleaner high-κ interface reduces charge traps, enabling near-thermal-limit switching, very small hysteresis, and vertically stacked complementary FETs. The contribution is the dielectric/channel interface and integration method—not a claim that 2D CFETs are ready to replace production silicon.
example: The reported long-channel MoS₂ devices averaged 68 mV per decade, with a best device at 61 mV/dec. A 5.8 nm A-TiO₂ device showed about 1.5 mV hysteresis in the reported sweep. The toy below multiplies subthreshold swing by required current decades; it does not reproduce transistor physics.

use_case.when: Study this result when evaluating low-power 2D logic research, especially the gate-dielectric interface that often limits switching and stability.
use_case.example: A device research team compares a crystalline transferred dielectric with amorphous HfO₂ for complementary 2D transistor stacks.
use_case.decision: Treat the paper as a device demonstration. Require yield, reliability, bias-temperature stability, contact resistance, process integration, contamination control, and independent replication before roadmap claims.

practice: Choose a measured subthreshold swing and current range. Predict the approximate gate-voltage swing in the toy relationship.
boundary: The calculator uses ΔV = subthreshold swing × decades as a teaching relationship. It does not simulate electrostatics, capacitance, leakage, contacts, variability, CFET interconnects, fabrication yield, temperature, lifetime, or production CMOS. Paper metrics are reported, not reproduced.

title: A secret reaches only the reusable workflow you pass it to
goal: Model secret propagation across nested GitHub reusable workflows without assuming transitive inheritance.
tag: CI/CD & GitHub Actions · reusable workflow security
concept:
Giving a hotel key to your travel coordinator does not automatically give it to the driver they hire.

GitHub reusable-workflow secrets pass only to the directly called workflow. In chain A → B → C, secrets: inherit on A → B makes secrets available to B. B must explicitly pass the required secret to C. Permissions also cannot be elevated as the chain descends.
example: Workflow A calls deployment workflow B with secrets: inherit. B calls cloud workflow C but passes no aws_role. C sees an empty or unavailable secret and must fail before deployment. The fix is an explicit B → C secret contract, ideally passing only the one value C needs.

use_case.when: Use explicit nested secret contracts when a reusable deployment workflow calls another reusable workflow that needs credentials or tokens.
use_case.example: A product pipeline calls a standard deployment workflow, which calls a cloud-specific AWS workflow requiring an OIDC role name.
use_case.decision: Pass the minimum named secret or input at every direct edge. Avoid broad inherit when a narrow contract works. Prefer OIDC for cloud access so long-lived credentials are not propagated at all.

practice: Toggle A → B inheritance and B → C forwarding. Predict which workflow can read aws_role.
boundary: The model uses sets of secret names. It does not run GitHub Actions, distinguish secrets from inputs, evaluate environments, mask logs, mint OIDC tokens, enforce repository access, reduce GITHUB_TOKEN permissions, or model organization policies.

title: Half-close ends your sends; cancel ends the gRPC call
goal: Distinguish finishing a client-stream from cancelling the RPC and its already-applied effects.
concept:
Sealing an envelope says “I am done adding pages; please answer.” Tearing up the conversation says “stop now.”

In a client-streaming gRPC, the client sends multiple messages and then half-closes its send side. The server can finish reading and return one response. Cancellation is different: it terminates the RPC immediately. Changes already made before cancellation are not rolled back automatically.
example: A client streams quantities 3, 4, and 5 for order o-51. Half-close lets the server return total 12. If the client cancels after 3 and 4, the third message is not sent, and any database effect already committed for the first two messages needs its own transaction or compensation design.

use_case.when: Use client streaming when one logical operation uploads an ordered sequence and the server should respond after the client finishes sending.
use_case.example: Stream data-quality rule fragments, half-close the request stream, then receive one compiled validation result.
use_case.decision: Use unary RPC for small bounded payloads. For streaming side effects, define commit boundaries, idempotency, deadline, cancellation cleanup, and partial-progress semantics before choosing the protocol.

practice: Choose half-close or cancel after two messages. Predict what the server may read, respond, and retain.
boundary: The model uses a local list and integer sum. It does not open HTTP/2 streams, apply flow control, run generated stubs, deliver metadata/status, enforce deadlines, observe races, persist transactions, retry, or guarantee when a real server notices cancellation.
